strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem—the parameter cost of Bayesian neural networks—with a clean, well-motivated parameterization (W = AB^T) that reduces variational parameters from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)).

Experimental coverage spans three architecture families (MLPs, LSTMs, Transformers) and multiple modalities (tabular/clinical, time series, text, image), with additional MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy-regression results in the appendix.
The appendix is unusually detailed on reproducibility (hardware, seeds, optimizers, KL scaling, priors, architectures), which supports partial reproduction.

The convex-hull/closure invariance argument (Proposition E.13) is a neat technical device that lets deterministic rank-sensitive Gaussian-complexity bounds transfer to the posterior predictive mean despite rank not being preserved under expectation.

The limitations section is honest about the calibration gap, tuning burden, and overlapping confidence intervals, and the OOD/selective-prediction gains on MIMIC-III and Beijing are a plausible and useful practical contribution.
The variance-preserving initialization derivation (Appendix F) is a sensible, if standard, treatment of the scale non-identifiability of the factorization.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical contribution—the 'singularity' of the induced posterior—is essentially a restatement of the trivial fact that a pushforward of a distribution through a rank-constrained map is supported on a Lebesgue-null set. The proof (Theorem 3.4) is immediate from Lemmas 3.2–3.3 and provides no new understanding; the paper's framing as a deep 'geometric distinction' from mean-field is oversold, and no experiment isolates any benefit attributable to singularity rather than to low-rank parameterization per se.

The PAC-Bayes 'improvement' (Theorem 3.8) reduces to parameter counting under the unjustified and unverified assumption that per-parameter KL divergences are equal across full-rank and low-rank posteriors (C_max^full = C_max^LR). No evidence is given that this holds; if the low-rank factors have larger per-parameter KL, the claimed tighter bound may not materialize.

The Gaussian-complexity results (Section 3.5) are explicitly admitted to be vacuous for both methods (Figure 3) and to provide no practical certificates, so they add little to the paper's claims beyond a formal transfer result.
The loss-approximation bounds (Theorems 3.6–3.7) are direct applications of Eckart-Young-Mirsky plus Lipschitz continuity—textbook steps rather than a novel theoretical insight.

The most directly comparable baselines are missing. Low-rank covariance methods (Swiatkowski et al., 2020; Tomczak et al., 2020), SWAG, and Bayesian-LoRA variants are discussed in the related-work table but never evaluated. The authors themselves concede this would 'strengthen the positioning,' yet it is central to the contribution claim.

Table 1 is numerically corrupted and unreadable: values such as '822 ± 803' for AUROC (a [0,1] quantity), '145 ± 636' for AUPR, and NLL '204 ± 617' have clearly lost their decimal points. The main MIMIC-III results are therefore not interpretable as presented.

The empirical claims of being 'competitive with Deep Ensembles' are weakly supported: on MIMIC-III, Low-Rank trails Deep Ensembles on AUROC (0.895 vs 0.929) and NLL (0.433 vs 0.300); on SST-2, accuracy (0.806) is below both the deterministic (0.812) and Deep Ensemble (0.825) baselines, and calibration is worse. The method's consistent advantage is largely limited to parameter efficiency and OOD detection.

There are internal inconsistencies across sections—e.g., Beijing dataset sizes are given as '6,260 validation, 6,260 test' in the main text but '7,553 validation, 7,553 test' in Appendix G.4—which undermine confidence in reproducibility.

The proposed mechanism linking the singular posterior geometry to improved OOD detection and calibration is correlational; no ablation isolates the effect of the rank constraint's 'correlation structure' versus generic low-rank regularization or reduced effective capacity.

Several figures (e.g., radar plots, trade-off scatter plots) are low-resolution and hard to interpret, and effect sizes for the reported gains are often within overlapping confidence intervals, as the authors acknowledge.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant problem (parameter-efficient Bayesian deep learning) and proposes a concrete, implementable low-rank variational parameterization with architecture-specific realizations for MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers.

The EYM-based decomposition of approximation error into learning error and rank bias (Theorems 3.6-3.7) and the covariance structure of factor-induced weight correlations (Lemma 3.5) are mathematically correct derivations as far as they go.

The appendix is extensive, providing implementation, initialization, and reproducibility details, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges overlapping confidence intervals and the absence of key baselines.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical claim (Theorem 3.4, 'singularity') is essentially trivial: any pushforward of a distribution over factors R^{m×r}×R^{n×r} under (A,B)->AB^T is supported on a lower-dimensional manifold and hence singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure. The 'proof by contradiction' just restates this basic measure-theory fact. More importantly, the paper never establishes any causal link between weight-space singularity and the claimed benefits (generalization, OOD detection); weight-space measure-theoretic singularity is largely vacuous for a BNN whose relevant object is a distribution over functions.

The Gaussian complexity contribution (Theorem 3.9) is self-defeating: the authors themselves state in Section 3.5 that 'the Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous for both methods and do not provide practical generalization certificates.' Presenting a central theorem the authors concede is non-informative is a serious significance problem. The transfer also relies on Assumption E.4 (almost-sure spectral norm bounds), which Gaussian posteriors violate, necessitating a large amount of patching (Sections E.10-E.11, added convexity assumptions) whose resulting bounds are looser still.

The PAC-Bayes 'tighter bound' (Theorem 3.8) hinges entirely on the unjustified assumption C_max^full = C_max^LR (per-parameter KL equal across parameterizations). Under this assumption the result is nothing more than a parameter-count argument dressed up as a generalization result; the per-parameter KL for low-rank factors is not shown to be comparable, so the claim of provably tighter guarantees is unsupported.

Theorem 3.7 (Eq. 4 in the main text) is dimensionally inconsistent: it adds ||W - W_r*||_F (a norm) to σ_{>r}^2 = sum of squared tail singular values. The appendix proof (C.6) uses the square root, sqrt(sum σ_i^2), so the main-text statement is simply wrong/inconsistent with its own proof.

The loss bounds address a single linear layer and do not compose to a deep nonlinear network; under the stated assumptions (L-Lipschitz loss, bounded inputs) they are direct consequences of Lipschitzness plus EYM and do not constitute meaningful generalization guarantees for the BNN.

The empirical evidence does not support the central claims. The paper admits confidence intervals overlap across seeds and that 'larger-scale studies with more seeds would be needed to establish statistical significance for smaller effect sizes.' The OOD improvements are marginal (e.g., MIMIC-III AUPR-In 0.824 vs. 0.807 for Full-Rank; SST-2 AUPR-In 0.302), while the method is clearly worse on the primary predictive metrics (MIMIC-III NLL 0.433 vs. Deep Ensemble 0.300; SST-2 accuracy 0.806 vs. 0.825).

The comparison to Deep Ensembles is set up favorably: a single low-rank model is compared against a 5-member ensemble, and the '15x fewer parameters' framing obscures that the single model loses on accuracy/calibration, which the abstract's 'competitive predictive performance' phrasing understates.

The results tables are visibly garbled/corrupted (e.g., Table 1 entries such as '822 ± 803', '145 ± 636', '195 ± 801'; Table 3 entries such as '812±.004', '496±.015'). This is a severe presentation and reproducibility defect that makes the reported numbers impossible to verify.

The paper omits the closest and most relevant baselines (SWAG, low-rank covariance methods of Tomczak et al. 2020 and Swiatkowski et al. 2020, MC-dropout), which the authors acknowledge only in passing. This undermines the positioning claim of being the first principled end-to-end low-rank BNN and leaves the contribution's incremental nature unclear.

The bibliography is riddled with author/year mismatches (e.g., 'Jordan et al. (2017)' for a 1999 paper, 'Chen et al. (2014)' for Stochastic Gradient HMC, 'Hinton et al. (2016) and Van Camp (1993)', 'Kingma and P. and Ba (2015)'), and several figures appear distorted/low-resolution, further degrading presentation quality.

strengths: Presents a simple and parameter-efficient low-rank variational inference framework for BNNs, reducing parameters from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)) while capturing structured weight correlations through shared latent factors.

The theoretical analysis is comprehensive and mathematically correct, covering the singularity of the induced posterior, covariance structure, Eckart-Young-Mirsky-based loss bounds, and PAC-Bayes / Gaussian complexity generalization bounds.

Empirical evaluation spans multiple architectures (MLPs, LSTMs, Transformers) and datasets (MIMIC-III, Beijing Air Quality, SST-2, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, toy regression), demonstrating parameter efficiency and competitive performance on several metrics.
The paper is honest about limitations, including the calibration-OOD detection tradeoff, tuning requirements for rank and KL weight, and overlapping confidence intervals across seeds.
The appendix provides extensive implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, seeds, preprocessing), which enhances reproducibility in principle.
The related work comparison (Appendix A) is thorough and clearly positions the method relative to prior low-rank BNN approaches.
weaknesses: The core idea—low-rank factorization of weight matrices in Bayesian neural networks—is not novel; closely related methods exist (e.g., low-rank covariance approximations, Bella, LoRA-Bayes), and the specific combination of BBB with mean-field over factors is straightforward.

The theoretical contributions are largely straightforward consequences of standard results. The singularity result is mathematically trivial (any distribution supported on a measure-zero set is singular). The PAC-Bayes bound reduces to a parameter-count comparison and is often vacuous (as Figure 3 shows). The Gaussian complexity bound is also vacuous, as the authors admit.

The experimental tables (Table 1 and Table 3) contain corrupted and impossible numbers (e.g., AUROC of 822, AUPR of 145, standard deviations larger than means, probability values > 1), and the text's reported values frequently do not match the tables (e.g., text says Low-Rank AUROC = 0.895 but Table 1 shows 195 ± 801). This severely undermines confidence in the experimental evidence and reproducibility.

The empirical claims are overstated: the method is not consistently competitive with deep ensembles, especially on calibration (NLL, ECE), which is a key metric for Bayesian methods. On SST-2, Deep Ensemble achieves 0.825 accuracy and 0.434 NLL vs. Low-Rank 0.806 and 0.527; on Beijing, Deep Ensemble MAE is 10.45 vs. Low-Rank 10.63.

The paper omits empirical comparison with the most relevant baselines: low-rank covariance methods (Tomczak et al., 2020; Swiatkowski et al., 2020), which are the closest competitors and are only discussed theoretically.

The singularity property is presented as a key contribution, but its practical benefit is not isolated from the low-rank constraint itself. No experiment separates the effect of singularity from the effect of parameter reduction.
No deterministic low-rank baseline is included, making it difficult to assess the benefit of the Bayesian treatment versus simply using a low-rank deterministic network.

Wall-clock efficiency gains are limited at small scale (Table 9 shows low-rank training time comparable to or slower than full-rank BBB) and only emerge at larger scale, limiting the practical impact for the small-to-medium architectures used in several experiments.

The PAC-Bayes bound comparison assumes equal C_max across full-rank and low-rank posteriors, which may not hold, and the bound is on the factor posterior rather than the induced W posterior, limiting the strength of the claimed generalization advantage.
The title and framing around 'singularity' oversell a mathematically trivial property, which may mislead readers about the depth of the theoretical contribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem: the O(mn) parameter cost of mean-field BNNs, and proposes a concrete, easy-to-implement low-rank factorization (W = AB^T with mean-field Gaussians on A and B) that reduces variational parameters to O(r(m+n)).

Demonstrates substantial and real parameter savings (up to ~33x vs a 5-member Deep Ensemble and ~13x vs full-rank BBB on SST-2, plus reduced peak GPU memory in the controlled profiling benchmark), which is a practically useful efficiency contribution.

Provides an extensive empirical study across MLPs (MIMIC-III), LSTMs (Beijing PM2.5), and Transformers (SST-2), including OOD detection, selective prediction, calibration, rank ablations, and SWAG comparisons, with multi-seed runs.

The limitations discussion is comparatively honest: the authors explicitly acknowledge the calibration gap vs ensembles, that Gaussian-complexity bounds are vacuous, that low-rank training is slower than full-rank BBB at small scale, and that some confidence intervals overlap across seeds.
The appendix is thorough and reproducibility-oriented (hardware, seeds, priors, KL scaling, initialization theory, architecture-specific implementation details).
weaknesses: The paper's headline theoretical contribution — 'singularity' of the induced posterior (Theorem 3.4) — is essentially trivial: any distribution supported on the rank-<=r set (a measure-zero subset of R^{m x n}) is automatically singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure. The proof follows immediately from Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3 and requires no substantive analysis. Framing this as a central 'Measure-Theoretic Singularity' result overstates the novelty and risks conflating it with Watanabe's singular learning theory (cited but unrelated to this measure-theoretic statement).

The empirical tables are inconsistent with the main text, which undermines confidence in the reported results. For example, Table 1 lists Deep Ensemble AUROC = 325 while the text states 0.929; Table 1 lists Low-Rank AUC-OOD = 382 while the text states 0.802; Table 3 lists Low-Rank accuracy = 606 while the text states 0.806 (decimal points appear stripped throughout, and some entries cannot be reconciled by a simple formatting fix). AUPR-Outs / arrow conventions also appear garbled. These are serious evidential/presentation problems for a results-driven paper.

Reported advantages are mixed and often not realized. Deep Ensembles are frequently stronger on key metrics (MIMIC-III NLL 0.300 vs 0.433; SST-2 accuracy 0.825 vs 0.806; Beijing MAE 10.45 vs 10.63), and the paper itself concludes the benefit is task-dependent and mostly limited to OOD detection / coverage / parameter efficiency. The abstract's claim of 'substantially improves OOD detection' is not uniformly supported across the three benchmarks.

Novelty is incremental. Placing variational distributions on low-rank factors is standard Bayesian low-rank matrix factorization / 'Bayesian LoRA from scratch'; the components (low-rank factorization, mean-field VI on factors, Lipschitz + Eckart-Young-Mirsky loss bounds, PAC-Bayes parameter-count arguments) are all textbook or straightforwardly adapted. The comparison table (Table 5) largely distinguishes the method by not requiring a pretrained backbone rather than by a fundamentally new mechanism.

The efficiency claim is weakened by the authors' own measurements: on MIMIC-III, low-rank training (532s) is slower than full-rank BBB (502s) despite 70% fewer parameters, so at small/medium scale the advantage is memory, not wall-clock. The abstract's 'significantly reduced computational cost' is thus only partially supported.

The generalization-bound story is weak in practice. The Gaussian-complexity bound (Theorem 3.9) is admitted to be vacuous, and the PAC-Bayes bound becomes vacuous above r ~ 11 (Figure 3), so the 'provably tighter' guarantees do not yield usable certificates for the regimes tested. Moreover, the PAC-Bayes ratio in Theorem 3.8 relies on the strong, unverified assumption that per-parameter KL terms are equal across the full-rank and low-rank parameterizations (C_max^full = C_max^LR); the actual learned KLs are not reported.

Some baselines appear suspiciously weak (e.g., Deep Ensemble PICP = 0.310 and Rank-1 PICP = 0.449 on Beijing Air Quality), which may inflate the relative coverage/calibration advantages attributed to the low-rank posterior. The lack of a more carefully tuned ensemble or SWAG in the main tables (SWAG is relegated to the appendix) limits the strength of the positioning.

The 'structured correlations' argument (Section 3.2 / Lemma 3.5) is a generic property of any factor model and does not by itself distinguish the approach from existing low-rank covariance methods; the claimed generalization benefit is asserted rather than demonstrated causally.

strengths: The core direction—fully end-to-end low-rank variational inference over factor matrices (W = AB^T) with posteriors learned from initialization across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers—is a reasonable and practically useful framing, and the resulting parameter/memory savings are real (e.g., 1.47M vs 19.84M vs 49.61M parameters on SST-2 with a controlled profiling benchmark).

The convex-hull/closure transfer argument (Lemma E.9–E.11, Prop. E.13) showing that the Bayesian posterior predictive mean lies in the closed convex hull of the rank-r support class and therefore inherits deterministic rank-sensitive Gaussian-complexity bounds is a genuine, if modest, technical contribution, and the Gaussian-complexity vs. PAC-Bayes comparison in Appendix E.9 is thoughtful.

The framework is architecture-agnostic and the paper provides extensive implementation detail (seeds, hardware, KL schedules, initialization derivation in Appendix F) that aids reproducibility in principle.
The paper includes an honest discussion of several limitations (calibration gap vs. ensembles, overlapping confidence intervals, single-run ensembling study, β/rank tuning), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are largely trivial or standard facts dressed up as significant contributions. Lemma 3.2/3.3 and Theorem 3.4 ("singularity") follow immediately from rank(AB^T) ≤ min(rank A, rank B) ≤ r and the standard fact that low-rank matrices have Lebesgue measure zero; the measure-theoretic framing adds little, and the "singular" terminology is potentially misleading relative to singular learning theory (Watanabe references appear in the bibliography but are never used).

Theorems 3.6/3.7 are direct consequences of Lipschitz continuity plus the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem; the "rank bias" term is the tail spectrum of the *learned* full-rank solution W*, which is itself a training artifact rather than a well-defined target, making the decomposition circular and non-actionable. Theorem 3.8 essentially restates that PAC-Bayes KL complexity scales with the number of parameters; the √(r(m+n)/mn) ratio is just a parameter-count ratio that ignores the possibility of a worse empirical-risk term, and the authors themselves note the bound is vacuous in practice (Fig. 3).

The empirical evidence does not support the central claims and contains internal contradictions. On MIMIC-III the text claims Low-Rank achieves AUC-OOD = 0.802 vs. 0.738 (Deep Ens.) and 0.770 (Full-Rank), but Table 1 reports AUC-OOD = 0.382 for Low-Rank vs. 0.758/0.750—a direct contradiction. Text AUROC figures (0.929 DE) also conflict with Table 1 (0.325 DE).

Tables 1 and 3 contain systematically corrupted/implausible entries (e.g., SST-2 accuracy of "606±103", MIMIC "325±0.0", "532±100"), which is a serious presentation and reproducibility failure and makes the reported numbers untrustworthy.

The method frequently loses on the very metrics it claims (OOD detection, NLL) to Deep Ensembles and SWAG; on SST-2 Deep Ensemble is stronger on both NLL and AUROC-OOD, and on Beijing Deep Ensemble is stronger on OOD AUROC. The "calibration–OOD tradeoff" narrative is repeatedly used to reinterpret losses as advantages without decisive evidence.

No empirical comparison is made to the most closely related methods—low-rank covariance VI (Tomczak et al. 2020; Swiatkowski et al. 2020) and Bayesian-LoRA/BLoB—even though these are discussed at length in the related-work table (Table 5). This is the key missing baseline for the paper's positioning.

Efficiency claims are oversold. At small/medium scale there is no wall-clock speedup (MIMIC-III: 532s vs. 502s for Full-Rank BBB—actually slower), and the headline "33× fewer parameters than Deep Ensembles" compares a single model to a 5-member ensemble; only a tiny BERT-mini-scale Transformer shows a speedup.

Baseline fairness is questionable: Full-Rank BBB underperforms dramatically (e.g., 0.752 accuracy on SST-2), which is attributed to Cinquin et al. rather than to tuning; if the mean-field and ensemble baselines are under-tuned, the comparisons are not meaningful.

Rank and KL weight are selected via per-dataset ablation (with test-adjacent validation), and several results are single-run or have overlapping confidence intervals, so most claimed improvements are not statistically established. Figures (Figs. 2, 3, 4, radar charts) appear illustrative rather than quantitative, further weakening verifiability.

strengths: The core method is simple and natural: parameterizing each weight matrix as W = AB^T with a mean-field posterior over the factors is easy to implement, drops parameters from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)), and integrates as drop-in layers for MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers.

The empirical study is broad, spanning tabular (MIMIC-III), time-series (Beijing PM2.5), text (SST-2), plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST and toy regression, across three architecture families, with controlled profiling of memory/time and rank sweeps.

The paper is comparatively honest about limitations: it explicitly concedes that Deep Ensembles remain stronger on in-distribution likelihood and that some confidence intervals overlap, and it frames the OOD/selective-prediction benefit as task-dependent rather than uniform.

The related-work positioning (Appendix A, Table 5) clearly distinguishes the method from low-rank covariance approximations, rank-1 perturbations, and LoRA-based Bayesian methods, and the EYM-based loss decomposition (Thm 3.7) is a valid, if loose, accounting of rank bias.
The conceptual connection between shared latent factors and non-trivial weight correlations (Lemma 3.5) gives an intuitive explanation for why the posterior differs from mean-field independence.
weaknesses: The headline 'singularity' result is mathematically trivial. Theorem 3.4 is an immediate consequence of the fact that the image of R^{m×r} × R^{n×r} under a smooth map is contained in a measure-zero set in R^{m×n}. Lemmas 3.2-3.3 are definitional; the 'measure-theoretic apparatus' adds no insight beyond 'the posterior has no density in the ambient space.' This is also potentially confused with Watanabe's singular learning theory (cited but unrelated).

The abstract/claims of 'provably tighter theoretical guarantees' are not adequately supported. The PAC-Bayes ratio (Thm 3.8) holds only under the unjustified assumption C_max^full = C_max^LR; the low-rank factors would generally require different per-parameter KL to reproduce full-rank weight statistics, and without this equality the complexity comparison can be unfavorable.

The Gaussian-complexity bound (Thm 3.9) is admitted to be vacuous ('bounds are vacuous for both methods and do not provide practical generalization certificates'), so Section 3.5 delivers no usable guarantee despite being presented as a contribution.

The loss approximation results are generic and loose: the rank-bias term sqrt(sum_{i>r} sigma_i^2) is not guaranteed small, and the learning-error term ||W - W_r^*||_F is left unbounded, so the bounds do not establish a meaningful accuracy guarantee. The displayed Eq. (3) also appears garbled.

The central empirical claims are weak relative to baselines. Deep Ensembles are frequently better (e.g., MIMIC-III AUROC 0.929 vs 0.895; SST-2 accuracy 0.825 vs 0.806; NLL consistently better), and the OOD-detection advantage is metric-dependent (only on MI-based metrics) and not robust across tasks. The clearest, reproducible benefit is parameter efficiency, not predictive or uncertainty quality.

Reproducibility and presentation concerns: the main results tables contain implausible/corrupted values (e.g., Table 1 accuracy/AUROC entries and Table 3 '606±103' accuracy inconsistent with the text's 0.806; many entries report ±0.0 std despite 'averaged over 5 runs'). Some reported results (low-rank ensembling, profiling) are single-run. These inconsistencies undermine trust in the numbers.

Efficiency claims are nuanced and partly contradictory: at small scale the low-rank model is slower than full-rank BBB (532s vs 502s) due to dual sampling/matmul overhead, and gains only emerge for the Transformer; the 'up to 33x fewer parameters' framing overstates the practical speed advantage.

Rank selection is an additional hyperparameter requiring ablation, and the SVD-initialized variant requires a pretrained deterministic model, partially contradicting the 'end-to-end from initialization without pretrained backbones' selling point.

Novelty is limited: low-rank variational inference for BNNs and low-rank parameterizations are known; the main new element (the singularity framing) is trivial, so the incremental contribution is not clearly above prior low-rank BNN work.
